content.text:
Insights look clean: over the last 72 hours there were **no errors and no resource-limit problems** in any of the five deployments, just 2 minor warnings.

| Deployment | Result |
|---|---|
| EU, AU, site (`harmless-narwhal-958`) | Healthy, nothing found |
| **US** | 1 write conflict in `sessions:start`, on the `rateLimits` table (Oct 6, 12:40) |
| **CA** | 1 write conflict in `sessions:start`, caused by a code push (`start_push`, Oct 6, 21:25) |

**What they mean:**
- **CA: nothing to fix.** A session started at the same moment new code was being pushed. Convex retried it automatically and it went through.
- **US: the only thing worth changing.** `sessions:start` updates a rate-limit counter ([sessions.ts:21](convex/sessions.ts:21) and [sessions.ts:25](convex/sessions.ts:25)). Two sessions starting at once can collide on the same counter, and Convex then retries one of them. Convex handled it fine; it's just a warning. There are two candidates:
  - `sessionStarts` is per user, so it only collides when **one person opens several tabs at once**, which is likely what happened while you were building. That's harmless.
  - `newUsers` is **one counter shared by everyone**. That's the one that would collide often under real traffic. The rate-limiter library's fix is `shards`, which spreads the counter across several documents. It's a one-line change in [convex/rateLimits.ts](convex/rateLimits.ts):
    ```ts
    newUsers: { kind: "token bucket", rate: 60, period: MINUTE, capacity: 60, shards: 4 }, // global
    ```

Insights only reports write conflicts and limit problems, not slow functions. From the logs, the slowest function this session was `sessions:start` at 90–140 ms in the US, and the busiest is `items:list`, which re-runs on every insert. That's by design.

content.text:
The column change is done and running on localhost (screenshot above). Here are your three questions in order.

### 1. What the dashboard numbers mean
It's the number of function calls across all your dev deployments: **127K** in total. `items.list` is **90K** of them. That's mostly fine, and here's why:

- **`items.list` re-runs after every insert,** because that's how Convex live queries stay up to date. 24K inserts × (1 fresh run + about 2 cached copies) ≈ 72K, and page loads and reconnects make up most of the rest.
- **Cached copies still count as function calls.** Each green dot in the logs column is one. They're cheap (no database reads) but they're counted.
- **`items.remove` (7.4K)** is from an older version of the app; it's no longer in the code.

So it's neither good nor bad: it's what a demo built to hammer inserts looks like. The thing to watch is that list calls grow with **inserts × open tabs**. At 127K for a whole day of heavy testing, you're well within the free tier's 1M calls a month. The count only becomes a problem with many visitors running big N.

### 2. Columns, done
- **browser** shows only this tab's stopwatch, e.g. `435 ms`. It shows "—" for rows this tab didn't time, such as after a reload.
- **logs** has a small "server" label above it and shows the list read from the dashboard, e.g. `12 ms ●●`. Hovering a cell shows the full server breakdown, e.g. `items:add 8 ms · items:list 12 ms read fresh · 2 served from cache`.
- **The tiles** now follow the browser time, so they have meaningful colours (green / lime / amber by distance) instead of being all green.

Typecheck and lint pass.

### 3. How to cut `items.list` calls

| Option | Saves | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Stop listening in hidden browser tabs** (skip the subscription while the tab isn't visible) | Every background tab's cached copy on every insert | None really. Runs already cancel when the tab is hidden. About 10 lines. |
| **Close extra tabs while testing** | The ●● dots right now are my preview tab, your 5173 tab and the hosted-site tab | Nothing to build |
| **Insert in batches** (one mutation adds all N rows) | List re-runs drop from N to 1 per run | Rows arrive together, so you lose per-row timing, which is the point of the demo. Only worth it as an optional mode. |

I'd do the first one; it's the only change that cuts calls without changing what the demo measures. Want me to add it?

what is this number exactly, 
759 ms 

is it the time it got to the browser from the request?

Yes. It's the full round trip as your browser saw it: from the moment the browser **sent** the insert until the browser **had the row**. If it's in the **browser** column or the "until browser saw it" line, it covers every step:

```
browser sends ─► travels to Sydney ─► waits behind earlier inserts ─► items:add runs ─► items:list re-runs ─► update travels back ─► browser has it
└──────────────────────────────────────────── 759 ms ────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

For an Australia row like yours, that splits roughly into:
- **Server work, about 20 ms:** `items:add` plus the `items:list` re-run. That's the big number on the card and the logs column.
- **Everything else, about 740 ms:** the trip to Sydney and back, plus any waiting in line. That's the **network** number on the card.

Two details:
- **It's a stopwatch, not a log value.** It's measured in [useRegionBench.ts](src/hooks/useRegionBench.ts): a timestamp just before sending, and another when the insert's promise resolves. Convex only resolves it once the live list already contains the new row, so "resolved" means the row is visible to you.
- **With N > 1, later rows include waiting time.** The 10 inserts are processed one after another in that region, so row 10 waits for rows 1–9. With **N = 1**, the number is just the trip there and back plus about 20 ms of server work.

It can't be split into "time to get there" and "time to get back" separately: that needs the browser's clock and the server's to agree, and they're about 100–200 ms apart here. So it's the full round trip.
isn't a little deceving

Yes, a bit. The number itself is measured correctly, but the labels around it suggest things it doesn't mean:

1. **"until browser saw it" sounds one-way.** It reads like "how long the write took to reach me", but it's a full **round trip**: to the region and back. Anyone watching from another browser sees roughly the trip *back* only, about half.
2. **It quietly includes waiting in line.** With N = 10 or 50, most rows wait behind the earlier inserts, so the median is inflated by queueing, and nothing on screen says so. Only the footer hint mentions it.
3. **It mostly measures *your* distance, not Convex.** About 740 of the 759 ms is the trip between your browser and Sydney. Only about 20 ms is Convex. A viewer could easily read "Australia: 759 ms" as "Convex is slow in Australia".
4. **Your own connection is baked in.** Your traffic exits through Berlin, with about 80 ms on the first hop alone, so the numbers aren't what someone in Sydney would see.

Ways to make it honest, cheapest first:

| Fix | What changes |
|---|---|
| **Rename the labels** | "browser" → "round trip", and "until browser saw it" → "round trip (send → visible)". The "network" number becomes "round trip outside Convex". |
| **Report the first insert separately** | The first insert of a run never queues, so showing it as "no queue: X ms" next to the median separates distance from queueing. |
| **Add an estimated one-way time** | "≈ one-way" = half the network time. That assumes the trip there and back take equally long, which is usually close, so it should be labelled as an estimate. |
| **Measure true one-way time** | Do the clock-offset step from before. That's the only way to get a real "time to reach you" number instead of an estimate. |

I'd do the first three together. They're small, and afterwards every number on screen says exactly what it measures. The fourth is the real fix if you want to show one-way delivery times. Which do you want?

content.text:
I committed everything to GitHub and deployed it to convex.site.

- **GitHub:** 3 new commits on PR #5 ([saranatour1/Convex-Regions#5](https://github.com/saranatour1/Convex-Regions/pull/5)), which still has the old Cloudflare check failing. I rewrote the PR description. `demo-recording/` stays uncommitted.
- **Deploy:** the code from these commits is on all 4 regional backends, and https://harmless-narwhal-958.convex.site serves the new build. On the live site, Europe is marked fastest from Berlin, the columns fill in, and there are no console errors. `.env.local` is unchanged.
- **Not my change, but in my commit:** someone removed the `returns` validators from `items.list` and `items.add` outside this session. The app works without them. They went into the logs commit, and the commit message says the edit was made outside this session. Tell me if you want them back.

## How it works

### 1. One insert, start to finish
You click **Insert 10**, and the browser sends 10 `items:add` calls to each region. For one row:

```
 browser                      Convex region (e.g. Sydney)                    browser
 ───────                      ───────────────────────────                    ───────
 sent ──────► (travel) ──► [wait behind earlier inserts] ─► items:add runs ─► commit
                                                          startedAt
                                                     ─► items:list re-runs ─► (travel) ──► row visible
                                                          ranAt                             received
```

The browser records four timestamps for each row:
- **sent:** the browser's clock, just before sending
- **startedAt:** the server's clock, when `items:add` began. `Date.now()` is frozen when a Convex function starts, so the function just returns it.
- **ranAt:** the server's clock, when `items:list` began the re-run that included the new row
- **received:** the browser's clock, when the insert's promise resolves. Convex only resolves it once your live data already contains the row.

### 2. The numbers on each card

| Label | How it's calculated | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Big number: "inside Convex"** | `ranAt − startedAt`, median | Server work only: running the add, committing, re-running the list. About 15–25 ms everywhere. |
| **round trip** | `received − sent`, median | The whole thing, as you experience it |
| **outside Convex** | round trip − inside Convex, per row, then the median | The trip there and back, plus waiting in line. Mostly distance. |
| **fastest** badge | lowest median **outside Convex** | Which region is effectively closest to you |

Subtracting is valid because each value is a duration measured on a single clock. The browser and the server clocks never get mixed, and here they differ by about 100–200 ms.

### 3. The table

| Column | Source | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **round trip** | This tab's stopwatch for that row. It shows "—" for rows this tab didn't insert or after a reload. | `499 ms` |
| **server › logs** | The Convex dashboard: how long the `items:list` re-run that delivered the row took | `SERVER 13 ms` |
| *(logs tooltip)* | Also from the dashboard: the `items:add` time, and how many other open tabs got that same list result from cache | `items:add 9 ms · items:list 13 ms read fresh · 1 served from cache` |

### 4. How the dashboard numbers get onto the rows
The browser can't read Convex logs, so `pnpm run logs:sync` does it on your machine:

1. **It follows each region's logs** with `convex logs`, using your CLI login.
2. **It finds each insert's `items:add` entry.** That function logs the new row's id, so the entry can be tied to its row.
3. **It finds the list run that delivered the row:** the first `items:list` that ran fresh after that add finished. Other open tabs got copies of the same run from cache; they share its exact start time, so they're easy to count. I checked this rule against the browser's own record of which run delivered each row: 40/40 matched.
4. **It writes the times onto the row** with one `serverTimes:record` call per region. The live list then pushes them to every open tab, about 10 s after the insert.

If the script isn't running, the logs column shows "—". A copy is running in the background in this session right now.

### 5. Hosting
- **The four regions** (US, EU, AU, CA) are separate Convex deployments. Each has the same backend code and its own `items` table.
- **The site** is served by Convex static hosting from a fifth deployment, `harmless-narwhal-958`. The browser connects straight to all four regions.
- **Deploying** means both halves:
  - `pnpm run push:all` updates the four regional backends.
  - The static-hosting upload publishes the frontend.

  Since `ec08d6b`, a frontend and backend from different commits break each other, so always deploy both together.

## Still open
- **Rate limits are paused** (`PAUSE_RATE_LIMITS`) on all four regions, which includes the public site.
- **`.env.local` still points at the US region.** That's why I targeted each deploy at the right deployment by hand.
- **PR #5 is still a draft,** and the Cloudflare check on it will keep failing until the Workers Builds integration is disconnected.

content.text:
It's **N separate calls**: Insert 10 sends 10 `items:add` calls to each region, 40 in total. Each call inserts one row.

- **Click:** [RunControls.tsx:21](src/components/RunControls.tsx:21) calls `insert(n)` for each of the 4 regions.
- **The loop:** [useRegionBench.ts:125-130](src/hooks/useRegionBench.ts:125) is a `for` loop that calls `add({ key, sessionToken })` once per row, without waiting for the previous one. All 10 leave the browser at once over the region's WebSocket.

On the server, though, they don't run at the same time. Convex runs one client's mutations **one after another, in the order sent**. That's why later rows have longer round trips: row 10 waits for rows 1–9 to finish first. It's the queueing the footer mentions ("bigger N: later writes also wait behind earlier ones"). It's also why every insert triggers its own `items:list` re-run, which is where the 90K list calls in the dashboard come from.

A single call with N rows (an `addMany`) would cut that to one mutation and one list re-run per region. But all N rows would arrive together with one shared time, and the per-row timing the demo is built around would be gone.
well can we try running the function on the server instead once when call the function itself?
Yes. There are two ways to do it, and they behave quite differently:

questions.question: With one call from the browser, how should the server do the N inserts?

options.label: One mutation, N rows (Recommended)
options.description: items.addMany inserts all N rows in a single transaction. 1 call and 1 list re-run instead of N each, so it cuts dashboard calls the most. All rows appear together with one shared time, and there's no queueing.

options.label: One call, server schedules N
options.description: The browser makes one call, and the server schedules N single-row inserts that run in parallel. Rows still arrive one by one and the list still re-runs about N times, but the browser no longer sends N requests or waits in its own queue.

content.text:
The one-call mode works, and it does what we wanted. In EU's logs:

```
items:addMany        12 ms   ← 1 call writes all 10 rows
items:list   fresh   13 ms   ← 1 list re-run for the whole batch (was 10)
items:list   cached          ← the other open tab gets a cached copy
```

That's **1 mutation and 1 list re-run per region instead of 10 of each**, so in 1 call mode it cuts `items.list` calls about N-fold.

**Comparison from Berlin, N = 10:**

| Region | Outside Convex: 10 calls (earlier) | Outside Convex: 1 call | Inside Convex: 1 call |
|---|---|---|---|
| Europe | 239 ms | **135 ms** | 63 ms |
| USA | 345 ms | **251 ms** | 39 ms |
| Canada | 394 ms | **262 ms** | 33 ms |
| Australia | 759 ms | **426 ms** | 79 ms |

- **Outside Convex drops a lot:** with one call there's no queue, so it's essentially a single trip there and back. That makes it the cleanest distance measure the app has.
- **Inside Convex goes up:** one transaction now writes all 10 rows, and the rate limiter charges 10 units at once.
- **Every row shows the same round trip,** because they arrive together. The Compare chart becomes a flat line per region.

**How it works:**
- **The toggle:** a **1 call** chip next to N. It's off by default, which keeps the current 10 separate calls.
- **The mutation:** with the chip on, each region gets one `items.addMany({ keys })` call ([convex/items.ts](convex/items.ts)). It inserts all rows in one transaction, logs each new id for the logs column, and charges N units against the write limit, so batching can't get around it. Max 100 rows.
- **The log sync** understands `items:addMany`, so every row in a batch gets the batch's server times. I restarted it with the new code.

One thing I noticed: **the log sync adds a few list calls of its own.** Each time it saves times onto rows, `items.list` re-runs for every open tab. That's about one extra re-run per flush (it batches many rows), so it's small, but it shows up on the dashboard.

The tab renders: a switch and four bulbs, all off. Clicking it, with one screenshot mid-flight and one after every bulb has landed:

The **Light bulb** tab works, and the app-wide cap is in place. I tested both directions on localhost with no console errors, and lint and typecheck pass.

### Light bulb tab
- **One switch for everyone.** Each region keeps one shared switch row. A click sends the same "on" or "off" write to all four regions at once, and anyone else watching sees their bulbs change too.
- **Each bulb is driven by its own region.** It changes the moment that region's update reaches your browser, so the order you see is the real order. While it waits, a pulse runs down its wire and a live counter ticks. When it lands, the time stops and gets a rank (1st–4th); the winner gets a green border.
- **Realistic filament.** Turning **on** heats up fast (about 0.15 s, dark → orange → white glow). Turning **off** cools more slowly (about 0.45 s, white → orange → dark red → dark), the afterglow a real filament has. In the off screenshot you can see three bulbs fading orange while Australia's is still fully lit, waiting for its update.
- **Results from Berlin:**

  | | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | **On** | Europe 195 ms | Canada 240 | USA 250 | Australia 471 |
  | **Off** | Europe 248 ms | Canada 258 | USA 266 | Australia 482 |

- **10 clicks per visitor per hour** (new `bulbClicks` limit). It applies even with `PAUSE_RATE_LIMITS` on, since it's part of the experiment. Once the limit is reached the page says: "That's your 10 clicks for this hour. Try again in X min."

### App-wide limit: 5,000 calls per hour
- **New `appCalls` limit, enforced in one place.** Every public mutation (inserts, deletes, network tests, location logs, bulb clicks) passes through `requireSession`, so that's where it's checked. `sessions:start` doesn't use it, so it gets its own check.
- **Always on,** even when `PAUSE_RATE_LIMITS` is set, since it's the safety net. It's split into shards (separate counters), so busy traffic doesn't create write conflicts.
- **When it's reached,** the page says: "The demo hit its hourly limit (5,000 calls per region). Try again in X min."

Two limits on the cap itself:
- **It's per region.** Each region is a separate deployment with its own counters, so in total it's 4 × 5,000.
- **Queries can't be capped.** Convex can't rate-limit queries, because they can't write anything. `items.list` re-runs only after writes, though, so capping writes caps those re-runs too.

**Not tested:** reaching either limit. That would lock this browser pane out of the bulb for an hour, or take 5,000 calls.

content.text:
The network test now runs the same connection checks as Convex's own tool, on all four regions. This is on the `fix-network-test` branch, uncommitted.

**Each region now runs 7 checks** (★ = new, from `get-convex/network-test`):

| Check | What it hits | Europe, from Berlin |
|---|---|---|
| WebSocket | `items.ping` query, 5 times | 128 ms |
| HTTP | `.convex.cloud/instance_name`, 5 times | 130 ms |
| ★ **HTTP action** | `GET /api/ping` on the region's `.convex.site`, 3 times | 134 ms |
| ★ **SSE stream** | `GET /api/sse`, 5 events 200 ms apart | 132 ms to first event · **streamed** |
| Echo 128 B / 4 MB | `.convex.cloud/echo` | 124 ms / 4.10 s · 1.0 MB/s |
| ★ **WS 1 MB** | a 1 MB message over the live WebSocket | 171 ms · 5.8 MB/s |

**Why these three:**
- **HTTP action** is the only check that touches the `.convex.site` domain, which some networks block separately from `.convex.cloud`.
- **SSE** checks that streamed events arrive spaced out. If a proxy or antivirus holds the stream back, they arrive bunched together, and the row turns amber and says **buffered**.
- **WS 1 MB** catches networks that drop large WebSocket messages.

**How it's built:**
- **Backend:** [convex/http.ts](convex/http.ts) has the `/ping` and `/sse` routes. They send the cross-origin header and touch no data. [convex/logs.ts](convex/logs.ts) adds `netPayload`, which returns the 1 MB message.
- **Why `netPayload` is a mutation:** it needs a session and counts against the 5,000-call cap, since a public query can't be rate-limited and would let anyone download unlimited 1 MB payloads.
- **Logging:** the new results are saved with each logged test (optional fields).
- **Browser side:** [src/lib/netTest.ts](src/lib/netTest.ts) runs the checks, and [NetworkBlock.tsx](src/components/NetworkBlock.tsx) shows the new rows.

**Left out:** the official tool's **proxied WebSocket** test. It sends traffic through a third-party proxy hosted on Railway, which would make our test depend on someone else's server.

**Checked:**
- `curl`: `/api/ping` returns 200 with CORS, and `/api/sse` streams about 200 ms apart.
- In the app: a full Europe run passed all 7 checks. The earlier full four-region run of the old checks also passed.
- Layout: I shortened the header and tightened the rows so all 7 fit; every card is 355/355 px, nothing clipped.
- Lint and typecheck pass.

**Deployed:** the backend is on all four regions. It's not committed, and convex.site doesn't have the new checks yet.

feat(network-test): add the connection checks from get-convex/network-test

The network test only timed two paths (a WebSocket query and HTTP on
.convex.cloud). Networks usually break on the other ways a browser talks to
Convex, so each region now also runs the checks Convex's own tool uses:

- HTTP action: GET /api/ping on the region's .convex.site (3 samples).
  The only check that touches the .site domain.
- SSE stream: GET /api/sse sends 5 events 200 ms apart. Shows time to the
  first event, and "buffered" (amber) if they arrive bunched together,
  which means a proxy or antivirus is holding the stream back.
- WS 1 MB: a 1 MB message over the live WebSocket, for networks that drop
  large frames. Served by logs.netPayload, a mutation, so it needs a
  session and counts against the app-wide cap (a public query would be
  unlimited egress).

The routes send CORS * and read no data. New results are saved on the
netTests log as optional fields. Left out: the tool's proxied-WebSocket
test, which depends on a third-party proxy.
